newsitem.title: UK: British market regulator vows to keep eye on ball.
newsitem.headline: British market regulator vows to keep eye on ball.

text.p: Britain's financial market regulator, the Securities and Futures Authority (SFA), on Monday vowed its standards will not be degraded during the transition to an enlarged super-regulator of which it will form part.

"It is vital...that whilst we are preparing for change we must not be distracted from the task in hand," said SFA chairman Nick Durlacher. "(We) are committed to ensuring...there is no degrading of regulatory standards and that our duty to investors and our obligations to the industry and Parliament are upheld."

Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown announced in May that the current self-regulatory agencies covering the markets, investment management and personal investment will be amalgamated with banking regulation, to be transferred from the Bank of England, in a new, enlarged Securities and Investments Board (SIB).
The new "super-SIB" will also regulate building societies and supervise the insurance industry.
Durlacher said the new SIB presented an opportunity to reduce complexity and overlap, enhance investor protection and reduce compliance costs.
"All involved must endeavour to ensure that aspiration is met by achievement," he added.
The Treasury said last week that the Bank of England bill, transferring the regulation of the banking industry to the new SIB, will be introduced after the summer recess.

A draft Financial Services bill to transfer the responsibilities of the current SROs, supervision of insurance companies and of mutually-owned organisations will be published for consultation in the summer of next year and is unlikely to become law before 1999.

The proposed new system has already provoked doubts from City practitioners and others who fear it will be an unwieldy and expensive exercise that will not materially improve the current regulatory regime.

Durlacher was speaking on the occasion of the SFA's annual report which highlighted the movement towards a more pragmatic and flexible application of regulation as opposed to a more rule-based approach.

It said its SABRE transaction monitoring system had helped alert the financial authorities to irregularities at Morgan Grenfell Asset Management which led the firm to be fined a record two million pounds.
SFA also said it has introduced a new refined risk assessment tool called FIBSPAM which allows SFA to pinpoint surveillance resources to where they are judged to be most needed.
Over the past year, SFA completed its high-profile actions nine former executives of the collapsed Barings bank, eight out of nine of which resulted in disciplinary action.

The SFA said recently it is continuing to study the case of major interest rate options losses at NatWest Markets, the investment banking arm of National Westminster Bank, and is reviewing the role of a number of individuals.
It is expected to announce a decision on any disciplinary action against individuals or NatWest in the next few months after the Serious Fraud Office (SFO) said last week it will not pursue the case.
